questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/62f33dab4305a41a0bc180231fef7015361dec4aac63f14c31fd48a39b8fcd68.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{2}{y}$ traversed between the points $(2,1)$ and $(\frac{1}{3},6),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{2}{t}.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 6
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 6$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4+{t}^{4}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=4x{y}^{2},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4(\frac{2}{t})(t)^{2} \\  & =8t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{6}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{6}8t\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{1}^{6}\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the line integral

$$
{\int }_{C}9{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}{\int }_{0}^{9}\boxed{}\,\text{d}t
$$

where $C$ is the segment of the line $3x=y$ traversed from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(3,9).$ Which of the following is the missing expression under the integral on the right?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
3x=y\,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{3}
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{t}{3}.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{t}{3},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le 9
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le 9$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{3})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{10}{9}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=9{x}^{2}y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9{(\frac{t}{3})}^{2}(t) \\  & =9(\frac{{t}^{2}}{9})(t) \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}9{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{9}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{t}^{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}{\int }_{0}^{9}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the line integral

$$
{\int }_{C}(2x-3y)\,\text{d}s=\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}t
$$

where $C$ is the segment of the line $\frac{x}{2}=1-\frac{3y}{2}$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(-4,2).$ Which of the following is the missing expression under the integral on the right?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{2}=1-\frac{3y}{2}\,⟹\,x=2-3y
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=2-3t.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2-3t,\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-3\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-3)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2x-3y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2-3t)-3t \\  & =4-9t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2x-3y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4-9t)\cdot \sqrt{10}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-9t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}4y{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $\frac{x}{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ traversed between the points $(0,1)$ and $(2,e),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,⟹\,x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡y
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le e
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le e$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{2}{t}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{t})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=4y{e}^{2x}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4y{e}^{2x} \\  & =4t{e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡t} \\  & =4t({t}^{4}) \\  & =4{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4y{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{e}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(4{t}^{5})\cdot \frac{1}{t}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+4}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{e}{t}^{4}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ traversed between the points $(0,1)$ and $(2,{e}^{2}),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le {e}^{2}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le {e}^{2}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}{|t|} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)={e}^{x}{y}^{2},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}){t}^{2} \\  & =(t){t}^{2} \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{t}^{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/02582b9146af7bfa73ade5c4bd26ec7102650f324fede161f98482153730e868.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{12x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the arc of the parabola $x={y}^{2}$ from $(1,1)$ to $(6,\sqrt{6}),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le \sqrt{6}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le \sqrt{6}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{12x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4{t}^{2}+1,$ $\text{d}u=8t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & =12{\int }_{5}^{25}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{5}^{25}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{5}^{25} \\  & =\sqrt{{25}^{3}}-\sqrt{{5}^{3}} \\  & =125-5\sqrt{5} \\  & =5(25-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{24x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the arc of the parabola ${y}^{2}=8x$ from $(0,0)$ to $(\frac{9}{8},3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
{y}^{2}=8x\,⟹\,x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{8},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le 3
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{8})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{4}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{t}{4})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{16}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{24x}{y}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{24x}{y} \\  & =\frac{24\cdot (\frac{{t}^{2}}{8})}{t} \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{24x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}3t\cdot \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}+16,$ $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{3}{8}{\int }_{16}^{25}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{16}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({25}^{3/2}-{16}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(125-64) \\  & =\frac{61}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}6{x}^{6}{e}^{-2y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x={e}^{y/2}$ from $(1,0)$ to $(\sqrt{2},\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)={e}^{t/2}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{t/2},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t/2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{e}^{t}}{4}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=6{x}^{6}{e}^{-2y}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6{x}^{6}{e}^{-2y} \\  & =6{({e}^{t/2})}^{6}{e}^{-2t} \\  & =6{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}6{x}^{6}{e}^{-2y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}6{e}^{t}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+4}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u={e}^{t}+4,$ $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+4}\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{5}^{6} \\  & =2({6}^{3/2}-{5}^{3/2}) \\  & =2(6\sqrt{6}-5\sqrt{5}) \\  & =12\sqrt{6}-10\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/46f2f23c1cc2cb2caacd3703665af673a52a7e876665c7ba9420ae72138e1068.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}x{y}^{6}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{2}{y}$ from $(2,1)$ to $(1,2),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{2}{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{4}+4}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=x{y}^{6},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2}{t}\cdot {t}^{6} \\  & =2{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{6}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2{t}^{5}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{4}+4,$ $\text{d}u=4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{5}^{20}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5}^{20}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{5}^{20} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\sqrt{{20}^{3}}-\sqrt{{5}^{3}}] \\  & =\frac{40\sqrt{5}-5\sqrt{5}}{3} \\  & =\frac{35\sqrt{5}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/8d060e257d74e6e0e6b7f35bfb89e9e974499059ddf4d029c0cace195ba67c13.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y-x}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the segment of the line $x=2y-4$ from $(0,2)$ to $(2,3),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2t-4.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2t-4,\,t⟩,\,2\le t\le 3
$$

Note that the domain $2\le t\le 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-4)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(2)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(2t-4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y-x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{4-t}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{4-t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4-t,$ $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{4-t}\,\text{d}t & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{2}^{1}\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\sqrt{5}{\int }_{2}^{1}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{1}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1] \\  & =\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-0] \\  & =\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/2e4e808d8264685f9b88c5b0052870174d8be3ed2a7195149d45552118186a49.png)

By setting $y = t$ where $t$ is a parameter, find a definite integral with respect to $t$ that is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{x}{y} \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the arc of the parabola $x = y^2$ traversed between the points $(1,1)$ and $(9 , 3),$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x = x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y = t,$ we have 

$$
x = x(t) = t^2.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t^2 , \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 1 \leq t \leq 3
$$

Note that the domain $1 \leq t \leq 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the endpoints on the path.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057794/assets/d0cebdd804ff244d037e14df6ec33efb86b522644f7b4addc688e27fd6a57e95.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} y^3e^{-x} \: \textrm{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x = \ln{y}$ from $(0, 1)$ to $\left(\dfrac32\ln 2 , 2\sqrt{2}\right),$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x = x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x = x(t) = \ln{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \ln{t}, \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 1 \leq t \leq 2\sqrt{2}
$$

Note that the domain $1 \leq t \leq 2\sqrt{2}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the endpoints on the path.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{|t|} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y) = y^3e^{-x},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t} \\  & ={t}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{3}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u = t^2 + 1,$ $\textrm{d}u = 2t \, \textrm{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{2}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\sqrt{{9}^{3}}-\sqrt{{2}^{3}}] \\  & =\frac{27-2\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
